  "title": "ContamCal: Bayesian Calibration of Contamination-Adjusted Benchmark Scores via Provenance-Augmented Item Response Theory",
  "core_problem": "Benchmark scores are increasingly unreliable because training data may contain semantic paraphrases of test items that evade n-gram decontamination, and RL post-training further conceals contamination signals while amplifying score inflation. While recent work characterizes contamination effects (dose-response curves, detection methods, IRT-based item quality, mitigation strategy failures), no existing method provides a principled statistical framework that takes per-item contamination exposure estimates and outputs calibrated benchmark scores with uncertainty bounds—answering the question 'what would this model's score be if it had never seen the test data?'",
  "opportunity": "Rephrased test items can inflate MMLU accuracy by 8-15 points while evading standard decontamination. RL post-training (GRPO) further amplifies contamination effects: Yang et al. (arXiv 2601.06103) show that GRPO not only resurfaces leaked information but inflates performance on uncontaminated counterparts (GSMPlus, HumanEval), while SFT inflates only contaminated tasks—making RL contamination uniquely dangerous. 'The Emperor's New Clothes in Benchmarking?' (ICML 2025) demonstrates that no existing mitigation strategy (across 20 strategies tested on 10 LLMs and 5 benchmarks) effectively balances fidelity and contamination resistance, motivating post-hoc calibration rather than benchmark modification. PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026) demonstrated that IRT can identify low-quality benchmark items, but does not model contamination explicitly or produce adjusted scores. HiBayES showed hierarchical Bayesian models improve LLM evaluation with proper uncertainty, but ignores contamination. The dose-response curve paper (arXiv 2601.04301) characterizes how contamination scales with model size and dosage, but does not calibrate scores. Self-Critique (arXiv 2510.09259) detects RL contamination with 30% AUC improvement over baselines, but does not adjust scores. KDS (ICML 2025) achieves near-perfect correlation with contamination levels but requires white-box fine-tuning access and has not been validated on RL-trained models. The clear gap: a contamination-augmented IRT framework that synthesizes detection signals into per-item exposure estimates and outputs Bayesian-calibrated scores with posterior credible intervals. With EMNLP 2026 explicitly inviting work on contamination and data governance (ARR deadline May 25, 2026), this fills a critical methodological gap.",
  "landscape": "Eight detection paradigms are now recognized: time-based partition, Min-K%++ membership inference (ICLR 2025), Time Travel guided completion (ICLR 2024), ConStat performance gaps (NeurIPS 2024), BIG-Bench canary memorization, Self-Critique entropy collapse for RL contamination (arXiv 2510.09259), hierarchical semantic detection (arXiv 2025, F1=0.76), and Kernel Divergence Score (KDS, ICML 2025) which achieves near-perfect Spearman correlation (0.99) with contamination levels by measuring kernel similarity matrix divergence before/after fine-tuning—though it requires white-box access with LoRA fine-tuning, has O(N²) complexity, and has not been validated post-RL. For score adjustment, DCR (EMNLP 2025) produces adjusted accuracy via fuzzy inference but lacks uncertainty bounds and does not handle RL contamination. Inference-Time Decontamination (EMNLP 2024 Findings) rewrites leaked samples at test time but operates during inference rather than post-hoc. 'The Emperor's New Clothes in Benchmarking?' (ICML 2025) systematically evaluates 20 BDC mitigation strategies across 10 LLMs and 5 benchmarks, finding that no strategy effectively balances fidelity and contamination resistance—strongly motivating post-hoc calibration approaches like ours. The dose-response paper (arXiv 2601.04301, NeurIPS 2025) fits scaling laws across contamination dosage (34M-344M models) but characterizes effects rather than calibrating scores. Yang et al. (arXiv 2601.06103) use the same models we plan to use (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B) for controlled contamination injection, finding that SFT inflates only contaminated tasks while GRPO inflates uncontaminated counterparts too—validating our experimental setup and providing a natural comparison point, but they characterize effects rather than calibrate scores. For psychometric evaluation, PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026 Oral) applies 4PL IRT with neural networks across 41,871 items on 11 benchmarks but does not model contamination as a covariate and provides point estimates without Bayesian uncertainty. ATLAS (arXiv 2511.04689) applies adaptive testing with IRT for efficient evaluation but does not address contamination. HiBayES (AISI, arXiv 2505.05602) demonstrates hierarchical Bayesian evaluation with credible intervals but ignores contamination. Han et al. (EACL 2026 Findings) quantify contamination in psychometric evaluations via item/evaluation memorization and target score matching, but do not use IRT or produce calibrated scores. The fragility paper (arXiv 2510.02386) shows GRPO conceals contamination signals by collapsing log-probability distributions—Min-K%++ and ConStat fail post-GRPO, but Self-Critique's entropy-based signal survives because it exploits policy collapse rather than probability gaps. The ICML 2025 paper 'How Much Can We Forget about Data Contamination' shows contamination persists in small models following standard scaling laws, making controlled experiments on 1B-3B models tractable and informative. The clear remaining gap: a principled Bayesian framework that (1) synthesizes multiple contamination signals (including RL-robust ones) into per-item exposure estimates and (2) extends IRT with a contamination covariate to produce calibrated adjusted scores with posterior credible intervals.",
  "approach": "We propose ContamCal, a two-stage framework for contamination-aware benchmark score calibration. Stage 1 (Multi-Signal Provenance Mapping): For each model-item pair, we compute contamination exposure scores by combining four complementary signals—(a) embedding-based semantic near-duplicate retrieval (FAISS + sentence transformers) against known training corpora, (b) Min-K%++ membership inference scores, (c) ConStat-style performance gap analysis between original and paraphrased items, and (d) Self-Critique entropy collapse detection for RL-post-trained models. Critically, we use training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to aggregate signals into a composite per-item contamination exposure score, avoiding the circularity of learned weights that would require labeled contamination ground truth. RRF ranks items by each signal independently and fuses ranks via reciprocal weighting (1/(k+rank)), which is robust to score scale differences across signals and requires no training data. We additionally report results with simple rank averaging and per-signal ablations to verify robustness. We include a signal survival analysis: we systematically evaluate which detection signals remain reliable after SFT vs. after RL post-training, directly addressing the fragility problem (arXiv 2510.02386) by showing that Self-Critique compensates where Min-K%++ and ConStat degrade. We also discuss KDS (ICML 2025) as a high-performing alternative signal but note it requires per-model LoRA fine-tuning (expensive for multi-model evaluation), has O(N²) complexity, and lacks RL robustness validation—making it complementary but not practical as a default signal in our multi-model framework. Stage 2 (Contamination-Augmented Bayesian IRT): We fit a hierarchical Bayesian 4PL IRT model augmented with a contamination covariate: P(correct_ij = 1) = c_j + (d_j - c_j) · σ(a_j(θ_i - b_j) + γ · exposure_ij), where θ_i is model ability, (a_j, b_j, c_j, d_j) are item parameters, exposure_ij is the per-item contamination score from Stage 1, and γ captures the contamination effect. Bayesian inference is performed via Stan's NUTS sampler (primary) with an explicit convergence fallback strategy: if NUTS produces divergent transitions or fails to converge within 24 hours (diagnosed via R-hat > 1.01, bulk/tail ESS checks, or >5% divergent transitions), we fall back to (1) Stan's ADVI (Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference) with fullrank approximation, which provides orders-of-magnitude speedup and has been shown effective for unidimensional IRT models, or (2) PyMC's fullrank ADVI as an alternative backend. We note that prior work (Luo et al. 2022) shows Stan's ADVI is reliable for item difficulty estimates in unidimensional IRT, and our model's contamination covariate γ enters linearly, which should not pose additional convergence challenges beyond standard IRT. Prior sensitivity analysis for γ: we use a weakly informative N(0, 1) prior and verify robustness by re-fitting with N(0, 0.5) and N(0, 2) priors—the ADVI fallback makes this feasible within our timeline since each VI fit takes minutes rather than hours. The calibrated score is computed by setting exposure = 0 and marginalizing: Acc_calibrated = E[P(correct | exposure=0)] with 95% credible intervals. This differs from PSN-IRT (which uses neural networks without contamination modeling or uncertainty), from DCR (which uses fuzzy inference without per-item tracking or uncertainty), and from HiBayES (which provides Bayesian uncertainty but ignores contamination). Validation: We use controlled SFT contamination injection on small models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Pythia-1B/1.4B, OLMo-1B) at 5 dosage levels (0%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% of benchmark items mixed as paraphrases into SFT data). Ground-truth uncontaminated accuracy is known from clean baselines, allowing us to verify that calibrated scores recover true performance within predicted credible intervals. We validate signal aggregation via leave-one-model-out cross-validation: for each held-out model, RRF weights are fixed (since RRF is training-free) and we verify that exposure scores on the held-out model predict actual contamination-driven score inflation. For the RL case, we frame this as an observational case study rather than full validation: we apply Self-Critique to existing instruction-tuned and RL-trained model families (Qwen2.5-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B/7B) to estimate their RL contamination exposure, and demonstrate that the ContamCal framework produces plausible calibrated scores with uncertainty bounds. We explicitly acknowledge that without ground-truth contamination labels for these RL models, the calibrated scores represent our framework's best estimate rather than validated corrections. We validate the SFT-trained component against DCR's adjusted accuracy on the same benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge) for external consistency, and compare our controlled injection results with the characterizations from Yang et al. (arXiv 2601.06103) who use the same Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B models. Concrete day-by-day timeline (14 days): Days 1-2: Implementation of Stage 1 pipeline (embedding retrieval, Min-K%++ integration, ConStat paraphrasing, Self-Critique), begin paper writing (intro, related work, method section). Days 3-6: Run SFT contamination injection experiments (5 dosage × 3 model sizes = 15 LoRA-SFT runs, parallelized across 2 GPUs; overlap detection signal computation on completed models while remaining SFT jobs run). Days 7-8: Run all 4 detection signals on all contaminated + clean models, compute RRF exposure scores. Days 9-10: Fit Bayesian IRT model (NUTS primary, ADVI fallback ready); run prior sensitivity analysis; compute calibrated scores. Days 11-12: RL observational case study (Self-Critique on existing models, IRT calibration). Run validation analyses (leave-one-model-out, DCR comparison). Days 13-14: Complete paper writing (experiments, results, discussion), generate figures and tables, internal review.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["ADVI DISCRIMINATION BIAS: Luo et al. (2022) shows Stan's ADVI is reliable for item difficulty estimates but systematically biased for item discrimination parameters in IRT models, with bias increasing with model dimensionality. The 4PL IRT model has discrimination (a_j) and asymptote (c_j, d_j) parameters that may be biased under ADVI fallback, potentially affecting calibrated scores. The proposal cites Luo et al. but only mentions reliability for difficulty estimates—the discrimination bias must be acknowledged and mitigated (e.g., 2PL fallback, or demonstration that γ estimation is robust to a_j bias).", "MISSING CONCURRENT WORK: 'Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration' (arXiv 2604.12843, April 2026) uses multidimensional IRT with anchor items for LLM benchmark calibration—directly relevant as concurrent IRT-for-LLM-evaluation work. Does not address contamination, so does not threaten novelty, but should be cited and distinguished.", "MISSING CONCURRENT WORK: 'Silicon Bureaucracy and AI Test-Oriented Education: Contamination Sensitivity and Score Confidence in LLM Benchmarks' (arXiv 2603.21636, March 2026) proposes an audit framework for score confidence under contamination perturbation. Addresses the same high-level problem (trustworthiness of contaminated benchmark scores) via a different approach (perturbation auditing vs. Bayesian calibration). Should be cited.", "SELF-CRITIQUE AUC MODESTY: Self-Critique achieves AUC of 0.60-0.70 on RL-contaminated models—above random but far from the near-perfect detection of KDS on SFT models. Per-item exposure scores derived from Self-Critique for RL models will carry substantial noise. The proposal should explicitly quantify how this noise propagates through the IRT calibration (e.g., via simulation or sensitivity analysis on exposure score noise).", "TIMELINE ZERO-MARGIN RISK: The 14-day plan accounts for no debugging, no data access issues, no unexpected convergence problems beyond the ADVI fallback. The conservative GPU estimates (LoRA SFT at ~3h per run for 0.5B-3B models, likely 30min-2h in reality) provide implicit compute buffer but not timeline buffer. Consider identifying one component that could be dropped or simplified if behind schedule (e.g., reduce from 3 to 2 benchmarks, or drop ARC-Challenge)."]
Feedback: The proposal has made excellent progress across three rounds—all FATAL issues from Round 1 are resolved, and all major issues from Round 2 (ADVI fallback, signal aggregation circularity, RL framing, KDS citation, day-by-day timeline) are comprehensively addressed. The remaining issues are minor and should push this over the pass threshold:

1. **Address ADVI discrimination bias**: Add a sentence acknowledging that Luo et al. (2022) found ADVI biased for discrimination parameters, not just reliable for difficulties. Propose a concrete mitigation: (a) test a 2PL IRT model as an additional fallback if 4PL+ADVI shows discrimination bias, and/or (b) run a quick simulation showing that γ (the contamination effect) estimation is robust to a_j bias since γ enters linearly and is the primary parameter of interest.

2. **Cite two concurrent works**: Add 'Growing Pains' (arXiv 2604.12843) as concurrent IRT-for-LLM work that validates the IRT approach but doesn't address contamination. Add 'Silicon Bureaucracy' (arXiv 2603.21636) as a complementary contamination-aware evaluation framework taking the auditing rather than calibration approach. Both strengthen the positioning.

3. **Quantify exposure score noise propagation**: Add a brief discussion or planned analysis of how Self-Critique's modest AUC (0.60-0.70) affects the precision of calibrated scores for RL models. This could be a simple sensitivity analysis: inject Gaussian noise into exposure scores at realistic levels and measure how much the calibrated score posterior widens. This would make the RL case study more rigorous.

4. **Add a scope reduction contingency**: Identify which component to simplify if behind schedule by Day 8 (e.g., reduce to 2 benchmarks, drop prior sensitivity from 3 to 2 priors, or simplify the RL case study to a single model family).

These are all addressable within a revision without changing the core method or experimental design.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

# Analysis of "Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking"

## (1) IRT Model Used
The paper employs **Multidimensional 2-Parameter Logistic IRT (MIRT 2PL)**. The model is expressed as:
> "P(yi=1∣θ)=exp(aiTθ+di)/1+exp(aiTθ+di)"

This allows items to load on multiple latent dimensions, with discrimination vector **ai** and difficulty intercept **di**.

## (2) Anchor Items & Fixed Parameter Calibration

**Anchor Selection:** Initial anchors are selected via clustering of IRT item representations, choosing representative items from each cluster rather than relying solely on discrimination scores.

**Technical Process:** When new datasets arrive, the method holds previously calibrated anchor parameters fixed while estimating only new item parameters. As stated: "previously learned item parameters are held fixed, and only the parameters of newly introduced items are estimated using reference models."

This preserves model ability estimates (θ) across calibration steps, maintaining score comparability.

## (3) Contamination Discussion

Contamination receives minimal treatment. The limitations section acknowledges: "anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration," but no solutions are proposed—only flagged as future work.

## (4) Relation to PSN-IRT
The paper makes **no mention** of PSN-IRT or related person-fit detection methods.

## (5) Key Acknowledged Limitations

- Evaluation limited to knowledge/reasoning tasks in English
- Binary item responses only; graded/open-ended formats require adaptations
- Assumes stable anchor statistical properties as models evolve
- Calibration cost increases with accumulated anchor sets
- Random model-test partitioning may underestimate generalization difficulty

## (6) Evaluated Benchmarks & Model Families

**Benchmarks:** Open LLM Leaderboard (6 datasets; 395 models) and MMLU (57 subject subsets; 428 models)

**Model Families:** The paper doesn't specify particular model families—it evaluates a broad pool of 400+ models without categorizing by family (e.g., GPT, Llama, etc.).

# Router-Worker Audit Framework for LLM Benchmarks

## Methodology

The framework compares two conditions using a router-worker architecture:

**Clean Baseline:** A single router transmits original problem information as completely as possible to a worker, who answers based solely on router output.

**Noisy Conditions:** Multiple parallel routers (r ∈ {1,2,...,M}) delete, rewrite, and perturb problems. Their outputs aggregate before reaching the worker. As router count increases, "deleted, rewritten, and perturbed fragments may be recombined" into semantic-neighbor cues.

The key metric is gain = noisy accuracy − clean baseline. Persistent positive gains suggest contamination-related memory activation rather than noise-induced improvement.

## Models and Benchmarks Tested

Twelve mainstream LLMs were evaluated:
- Qwen series (3-Next-80B, 3.5-122B, 3.5-35B, 3-30B, 3-8B)
- Llama series (3.3-70B, 3.1-8B, 3.2-3B)
- DeepSeek (V3.2, Chat)
- Seed series (2.0-Lite, 1.6-Flash)

The study used "a fixed sample of n=100 questions" from a multiple-choice test benchmark.

## Key Quantitative Results

**Aggregate level:** At r=8 routers, "10 out of 12 models rise above the baseline" with mean positive excess of 0.066. By r=9, positive excess reached 0.086 (largest across all settings).

**Model heterogeneity:** Violation breadth ranged from 1/9 to 9/9 routers. Qwen3.5-35B showed maximum positive excess of 0.260, while Qwen3-Next-80B violated baseline in all 9 settings but with smaller jumps.

**Question-level transitions:** Wrong-to-correct transitions increased from 112 (r=1) to 180 (r=9), while correct-to-wrong decreased from 150 to 116, indicating "directional reversal" favoring improvement.

## Output Type: Audit Flags Only

The framework produces **audit flags and credibility assessments rather than adjusted scores**. It identifies contamination sensitivity patterns but doesn't recalibrate benchmark scores. The authors argue similar scores may have "substantially different levels of confidence" without proposing numerical adjustments.

## Distinction from Bayesian IRT Approaches

This framework differs fundamentally from Item Response Theory calibration:

- **IRT estimates:** Latent ability parameters and item difficulty through probabilistic modeling
- **Router-Worker method:** Empirically tests whether performance degrades gracefully under controlled information deletion, using pattern analysis rather than probabilistic inference

The approach is procedurally diagnostic rather than theoretically parametric.

## Acknowledged Limitations

The paper provides limited explicit limitation discussion but indicates constraints through design choices:

- Single benchmark dataset (100 questions from one test)
- Same model used for both router and worker roles
- Noisy conditions employ deletion/rewriting rather than adversarial perturbations
- No analysis of which contamination types (paraphrases, fragments, synthetic variants) most affect models
- No guidance on determining acceptable violation thresholds for deployment decisions

# Analysis of Self-Critique AUC Performance and Measurement Details

## AUC Numbers Across Models

The paper reports Self-Critique AUC scores at the **dataset level** (aggregated across all samples in each benchmark):

- **Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**: 0.70 average AUC across four tasks (AIME24: 0.72, AIME25: 0.72, K&K: 0.66, SAT: 0.67)
- **DeepSeek-Math-7B-Instruct**: 0.64 average AUC (AIME24: 0.67, AIME25: 0.61, K&K: 0.63, SAT: 0.67)

Results also appear for other model sizes in appendices.

## Measurement Level

The paper explicitly states these are aggregated metrics: "we primarily report the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), a standard metric for detection problems." The ROC curve construction necessarily requires aggregating per-sample scores across the full dataset.

## Noise and Per-Item Precision

The paper provides **limited discussion of per-item detection noise**. It briefly mentions in Appendix G.1: "Discussion on Result Variability and Error Bars," but the main text focuses on aggregate performance rather than individual prediction confidence or variance.

## Entropy Collapse Metric

The core metric uses: "token-level entropy is H_t = -∑_{v∈V} p_θ(v|x_{<t}) log p_θ(v|x_{<t})," then compares entropy sequences via "penalized cosine similarity" between two response entropy curves to generate contamination scores.

The paper acknowledges limitations regarding generalization and scalability in Appendix H but does not extensively address per-item detection precision variability.

## Stan and Bayesian Measurement Error Models

A Bayesian approach to measurement error can be formulated directly by treating the true quantities being measured as missing data, which requires a model of how the measurements are derived from the true values.

In Stan implementations, the true values are declared as parameters rather than data, the observed measurements are treated as data, the measurement error is specified as normal with a noise scale parameter, and the true values are given a hierarchical prior.

## IRT for Measurement Error in Predictors

It has been shown that measurement error in predictor variables can be modeled using item response theory (IRT), where the predictor variables that may be defined at any level of a hierarchical regression model are treated as latent variables.

## Differential Covariate Measurement Error

Bayesian hierarchical modeling approaches have been developed to account for differential covariate measurement error, particularly where the magnitude of measurement error differs by treatment status.

The search results indicate that Stan documentation provides guidance on implementing Bayesian measurement error models, and there is established research on combining IRT with hierarchical regression to handle noisy predictors.
